meta.title: Putin's Propaganda Machine: Soft Power and Russian Foreign Policy
meta.author: Marcel H. Van Herpen

parts.title: Introduction to Russia's Propaganda Tactics

sentences: **Introduction:** This section sheds light on the Russian **propaganda** machinery during the **2014 Ukraine Conflict**.
It parallels the Soviet **disinformation tactics** of the past, highlighting how it mixes **truths**, **half truths**, and **falsehoods** effectively.
Precedent from the **Soviet era** like **Lenin** and the **KGB's** operations is drawn to depict the evolution of information control under **Putin**.

With an emphasis on **modern media** usage, it elaborates crucial shifts in **tactics** and cites **real world examples** of their implications while warning about challenges to **Western public perception**.

parts.title: Russia's Information War and Propaganda Tactics

paragraphs.heading: Russia's Information War and Propaganda Tactics
sentences: **Igor Panarin** presents a **conspiracy theory** suggesting that the **Soviet Union's fall** stemmed from a **Western secret plan**, labeling it the "**First Global Information War.**"
According to Panarin, countries like the **US and UK** orchestrated this to damage the USSR, starting in 1943.
He alleges that **Nikita Khrushchev** and **Mikhail Gorbachev's** leadership were part of this operation, facilitated by Western secret agencies.

This narrative reflects a broader belief in a **Western conspiracy** in Russian thought, illustrated in Panarin and **Aleksandr Dugin’s** works, the latter of whom depicts a world caught in mystical conspiracies.
Russia **reinterprets post-Soviet events** as a periodic continuation of this supposed information warfare.
Efforts to **enhance domestic control** and **propaganda abroad,** like funding RT and launching channels in various languages, are viewed as part of a **defensive strategy.**
Panarin foresees the "**second information war**" concluding with a **Russian triumph** if the political elite engage in an "uncompromising informational-psychological" conflict.
Consequently, since 2012, Putin has enhanced **media control** and **restricted** NGOs, perpetuating a narrative against foreign "**negative information flows**."

parts.title: Russia's Soft-Power Strategy Revealed

sentences: Russia's "**soft-power offensive**" focuses on three strategies:
**Mimesis**: Russia mirrors **Western soft-power** tactics, creating organizations similar to Freedom House, like the **Institute for Democracy and Cooperation** (IDC).
These entities promote Russia's view on democracy and human rights, often contrasting Western values.
**Rollback**: This involves reducing **Western influence** inside Russia by limiting activities of Western soft-power institutions.

Russia sets up bodies like **Rossotrudnichestvo** and **Russkiy Mir** to project its power, especially within the former **Soviet Union**, and focus on **geopolitical clout** rather than cultural exchange.
**Invention**: This includes crafting novel strategies that exploit **Western openness**.
Tactics range from public relations campaigns to covert operations, mimicking past KGB techniques for a broader **global influence.**

parts.title: International Expansion of Russian Cultural Centers

sentences: **Russkiy Mir** sees "**Russian World**" as a global community, including **ethnic Russians**, **Russian speakers**, and **Orthodox believers** worldwide.
It sets up **Russian centers** in universities abroad, resembling China's **Confucius Institutes**.
Like Confucius Institutes, these centers on campuses aim to **expand influence** but with ties to Russian government interests.
**Critics** raise concerns about such centers, saying they could foster **propaganda** and limit **academic freedom**.
Unlike other Western cultural diplomacy organizations, these Russian initiatives are directly tied to the **government** and have **political motives**.

parts.title: Soviet Propaganda Tactics and Their Evolution

sentences: **Kremlin's propaganda** tactics used previously during the Soviet era evolved post-fall of communism.
Back then, **overt propaganda** involved mediums like Radio Moscow, Soviet magazines, and colorful stories about Soviet achievements.
However, it mostly reached those already sympathetic to the Soviet cause.
**Covert propaganda** had more hidden avenues like front organizations that appeared non-communist to hide the Soviet connection.
Meanwhile, **"fellow travelers"**—intellectuals who were not communists but showed naivety towards the regime—also disseminated propaganda.
Notable examples include **George Bernard Shaw** and **Sydney & Beatrice Webb**, who praised the Soviet regime despite its flaws.
This was principally a time when Soviet propaganda had limited access to Western media.
However, after the collapse of communism, this scenario changed.
**Russia's conversion to capitalism and democracy** altered its global image, allowing **greater media access**.
This change meant that while Russia did not become a completely friendly power, it did gain a significant foothold within Western media, unlike during the communist era.
Consequently, this established a more normalized international presence.

parts.title: Russia's Soft Power and RT Influence

sentences: **Russia** increased **use of "soft power"** by leveraging various tools, such as propaganda and **media influence**.

During the **Soviet-era**, their power relied heavily on military might, but **today**, Russia is utilizing its **cultural and historical ties** with neighboring countries and Russian-language communities.
The **Kremlin** also **contracted Western PR firms** and organized major conferences to influence foreign opinion.
This was part of a broader **propaganda strategy** to shape its international image and **actively engage in the Western media landscape**.
The launch of the **Russia Today (RT)** **English** channel exemplifies this push into global media.
From its inception, **RT** sought to challenge prominent networks like **CNN and BBC**.
Despite its **official affiliation**, RT presented itself with diverse and often **controversial content**, which included anti-US rhetoric and promotion of **conspiracy theories**.
The channel **invited extreme viewpoints** and was achieved a significant presence **online and on YouTube**.

This massive investment is indicative of Russia's determination to use media as an **instrument for influence**, aiming to reshape perceptions and drive a wedge between **Europe and the USA** over conflicts such as those in Ukraine.
**RT** serves as an impressive example of **contemporary propaganda**, presenting news heavily slanted to serve **Russian state interests.**

parts.title: Russian Influence in Western Media: The Lebedev Case

sentences: **Lebedev** was a former **KGB** officer turned **media owner**, acquiring stakes in the British papers **London Evening Standard** and **The Independent**.
He claimed his intention wasn't to make money but to "**waste money**" by supporting **loss-making** publications.
Despite promises of **editorial independence**, concerns arose about his **Kremlin ties**, especially after he received funds directly sanctioned by **Vladimir Putin**.
Though voted out of **United Russia**, he still preserved a **semidissident** image, backing **anti-corruption** efforts in Russia.
Lebedev's strategy mirrored **Pugachev's** in France, as they both took on **loss-making** newspapers with the intention of building **media empires**.
Both used a **father-and-son dynamic** for management.

Distinctly, while **Pugachev failed** due to financial and editorial challenges, **Lebedev** managed a **profit with the Evening Standard** by making it a **free paper**, showcasing **more adept management**.
Despite ongoing vigilance regarding **Kremlin influence**, **Lebedev** and his son became prominent figures in the **British media landscape**.

parts.title: Soviet Influence in Foreign Politics and Recent Infiltrations

sentences: **Soviet Influence in Foreign Politics** During **Soviet times**, the Kremlin financially supported foreign political parties and politicians.
An example is **Finnish President Urho Kekkonen**, who received **millions from Moscow** for his campaign and personal expenses.
Post-Soviet Russia, although losing control over **communist parties**, began influencing **"bourgeois" parties** in the West.
This approach was **less visible and secretive** but became **effective**, targeting new political systems that were not previously approachable.

**Recent Examples of Infiltration** Hélène Blanc and Renata Lesnik highlight **intensified Russian infiltration** in Europe, citing a 2002 example where **French candidate François Bayrou** was offered a funded campaign by unknown Russians.
Despite refusing, it revealed vulnerabilities in **political funding regulations**.
Interpol warned that alongside terrorism, Europe faces threats from **ex-Soviet businessmen** seeking political power.
Funds typically come through **European banks**, masking Moscow's involvement, as seen in **Netherlands and France**.

parts.title: Modern Russian Espionage Tactics

sentences: Russian espionage has seen **high-profile infiltration** within the **US and Europe**, with **aggressive efforts** targeting officials and politicians.
Russian spies often **pose as diplomats** or use **fake identities** to gather sensitive information.
Back in the **Soviet era**, Russian embassies used a significant portion of their staff for espionage.

In modern times, **Russian espionage** continues to be **persistent and sophisticated**, reflecting Cold War levels of activity, targeting post-Soviet and European states such as **Estonia** and the **Czech Republic** for **valuable information**.

parts.title: Kremlin & Orthodox Church Assault on Universal Human Rights

sentences: In recent years, **Russian foreign policy** has increasingly integrated "**traditional values**," particularly against **universal human rights**.
The Russian **Orthodox Church** (ROC) and the Kremlin have worked closely, attacking human rights in various international forums.
They argue that such rights should be implemented with respect to **cultural specificities**.
This has sparked debates regarding **controversial issues** like **reproductive rights** and **LGBT rights**.

The ROC's critique formalized in a 2008 document emphasizes that human rights shouldn't override religious traditions, leading to strategic movements in UN meetings to promote **traditional values** over global norms.

The joint efforts between the **Kremlin** and the ROC aim to redefine global ideological influences towards a "**Russian World**," using **Russkiy Mir Foundation** to spread Russian culture and **Orthodoxy** abroad.
This new strategy echoes Soviet times but targets the Russian **diaspora** instead of international communists, indicating a focus on **nationalism** and **conservativism**.

Their efforts are most visible when defending **Russian interests** and countering Western ideologies in international spaces, despite significant **resistance** from entities like the **EU** and the **UN Human Rights Council** against restrictive practices on **minority rights**.

parts.title: Russian Orthodox Church and State Subordination

sentences: **Russian Orthodox Church** is being used by the **Kremlin** for soft-power influence, spreading **neoimperialist ideology**.
It lacks independence from the **state**, failing to be a moral authority due to its history of subordination to state power.
This **subservience** hinders its role as a universal standard-bearer of **morality** or human rights.
Historically, this connection to state power has distorted its **moral influence**, as seen during **Chechen conflicts**.
The ROC also stood by during the **Maidan revolt** in Ukraine, aligning with state views rather than upholding independent moral standing.

parts.title: The ROC's Restrictive Role in Religious Freedom

sentences: The **Russian Orthodox Church** (ROC) is characterized by a profound **illiberal ideology**, mostly reserving **religious freedom** for itself, and actively working to restrict it for other denominations.
Post-Soviet attempts by the ROC to limit new religious entrants highlighted its opposition to **religious pluralism**.
This stance gained momentum with **Russia's government** and **intelligence agencies**, which framed foreign missionaries as agents of espionage.

By 1997, a new law discriminatory to "minority religions" like Protestantism and Catholicism was enacted, enforcing stringent registration processes that marginalized and criminalized groups like the **Salvation Army** and **Jehovah’s Witnesses** under the guise of combating extremism.

parts.title: German Political Elite's Pro-Russian Sentiment

sentences: **German** elites, especially **politicians** and **media**, show significant **tolerance** towards Russia's **hardline** politics, possibly due to **historical guilt** over WWII.
Former SPD Chancellor **Gerhard Schröder** exemplifies the **pro-Russian** sentiment; he maintains a **close friendship** with **Putin**, highlighted by personal **interventions**.
After his political career, Schröder controversially took a role with **Nord Stream**, a **Gazprom** project, provoking criticism for potential **conflict of interest**.
**Frank-Walter Steinmeier**, another key figure, is known for his **pro-Kremlin stance**.

**Promoted** within Schröder's circle, he later became **Foreign Minister**, backing policies **favorable** to Russia, such as opposing Ukraine and Georgia’s **NATO** membership due to "frozen conflicts."
This stance risked tension with **Western allies**, especially as it conflicted with **US policies** as expressed by Condoleezza Rice.

parts.title: Pro-Russia Bias in German Politics and Society

sentences: ## Pro-Russia Bias in German Politics and Society
German political figures and public attitudes have shown an inclination toward **Russia-friendly** policies.
Largely due to historical ties and economic **interdependence**, this bias can be seen across the political spectrum, from the **SPD** (Social Democratic Party) to **extreme** parties on both ends.
For instance, Steinmeier's calls for **dialogue** with Moscow often overshadowed **calls for sanctions** after Russian aggression.
Even Chancellor Merkel found herself at odds with him at times over these issues.
**Nostalgia** for Eastern German-Russian ties also manifests in former GDR perspectives that favor Russian alliances over Western ones.
This is evident by figures like Helmut Schmidt resisting condemnation of Russia despite its aggressive moves internationally.
Besides political figures, **organizations** like the German-Russian Forum also reflect these sentiments.
Former East German leaders serve on its board, propagating **friendly** relations based on historical & economic engagement.
This tendency echoes in businesses like **E.ON Ruhrgas**, showing strong ties to Russian energy through **interlocking** interests.
Prominent figures who were once part of the **East German regime** have moved into roles facilitating Russo-Germanic contracts, suggesting a systematic **interdependence**.
However, critics argue these associations often **underestimate** the implications of Putin’s policies and seek to **downplay** measures needed to uphold **European security** and cohesion.
Such attitudes risk reinforcing Russia's **geopolitical ambitions** at the expense of broader **European unity**.

parts.title: German-Russian Relations Impact on Foreign Policy

sentences: **German-Government Influence**: Germany's **relations** with **Russia** have impacted its **foreign policy**, particularly with the US, NATO, and Eastern Europe.
**Chancellor Schröder** weakened ties with the US by adopting a **"Russia first" strategy**, which led to criticism.

This **ambivalence** continued under Angela **Merkel**, causing **tensions** with NATO, as **Germany protested** against US proposals like NATO **Membership Action Plans** for **Ukraine** and **Georgia**.
**European Concerns**: Germany's potential shift toward Russia worries **Eastern Europe**.
Historical tensions with **Poland** and other neighbors may rekindle due to Germany's **military collaboration** with Russia, reminiscent of past **cooperation** in the 1920s.
This closeness with Russia undermines its role as a **reliable partner** for the US and EU, highlighting a **risks** of loosening ties with Western countries.

parts.title: France-Russia Relations: Evolving Strategic Partnership

sentences: The **relationship** between **France** and **Russia** has evolved, showcasing a **mutual friendship** that began under **Chirac** and continued with **Sarkozy**.

Despite **initial concerns** regarding **human rights** in **Russia** during the **Chechnya conflict**, **France** pursued **stronger ties** with **Moscow** during the **Iraq war**, aligning against the **US intervention**.
The partnership deepened with the awarding of **orders** like the **Légion d’honneur** to **Putin**, sparking **controversy**.
Under **Sarkozy**, despite his initial **stance** on human rights, **French diplomacy** leaned towards **practical relations** with **Russia**.
The **Mistral deal** exemplified this partnership, marking a significant **arms sale** from a **NATO** country to **Russia**.
This **sale** drew **criticism** from other **NATO allies** like **Poland** due to the sale's potential impact on European security.
In the diplomatic sphere, **France** pursued an **EU-Russia security collaboration**, which alarmed **diplomats** by seeming to **detach** from the traditional **US**-**EU alliance**.

**Sarkozy's administration**, while **acknowledging** global security intricacies, sought to align **France** more closely with **Moscow's** strategic interests, symbolizing a larger **shift** in **European geopolitical** dynamics.

parts.title: The Kremlin’s Influence in France and Europe

sentences: The Kremlin has made notable progress in improving its image, despite *aggression* in Ukraine straining relations with France, especially under socialist President François Hollande.
Initially more skeptical than Sarkozy, Hollande still maintained **economic cooperation** with Russia, signaling a pragmatic approach.

Putin’s personal diplomacy, combined with economic ties through **French energy giant Total** and think tank IFRI’s **indirect influence**, illustrated how deeply embedded Russia’s ties were with French **political and business elites**.
This alliance complicated the EU's response to Russia’s actions, highlighting how deeply **financial and strategic interests** were entwined.
Russian soft power efforts expanded beyond France, aiming for a strategic **Berlin-Moscow-Paris triangle** to counter U.S. influence in Europe.

This strategy leveraged sympathetic political parties, particularly in **extreme political spectrums**, showing Russia’s attempts to shape European geopolitics by forging alliances and sympathies across **political divides**.

Ideological admiration and **financial ties** further reinforced Russia’s influence, even as EU nations sought to balance strategic interests against growing concerns over Russia's **revisionist tendencies**.

parts.title: Combating Propaganda and Trolls

sentences: **Lithuania** and **Latvia** have taken steps to limit Russian media following **propaganda accusations**, such as banning **NTV Mir** and suspending **Rossiya RTR**.
Countries like **Estonia** prefer **counter-programming** over strict bans to combat this media influence, producing content in their local languages instead.
The Kremlin employs **online trolls** to spread **pro-Kremlin messages**, often causing **chaos in internet forums**.
Papers like the **Moscow Times** have disabled comment sections due to such disruptive activity.
**Recognizing** these trolls can be challenging, yet **blacklists** could serve as a solution.
Western governments might consider agencies dedicated to identifying and addressing **Kremlin's digital misinformation**.

parts.title: Russian Orthodox Church and the KGB's Role in Modern Geopolitics

sentences: **The Russian Orthodox Church**, acting as a global church, has substantial relations with the **KGB**, which historically included a coup d'état and the First Chief Directorate of KGB.
**Patrick Johnstone** and **Metropolitan Anthony** appear within this network, emphasizing the church's expansive links and influences over time.
On a geopolitical note, **Kaliningrad** is crucial, hosting **military exercises like Kavkaz-2012**.
Leaders such as **Kadyrov**, **Patriarch Kirill**, and entities like **LukOil** remind us of Russia's political and energy power plays.

The **KGB’s** influence extends beyond traditional espionage, impacting modern political and religious narratives, illustrating a blend of **politics, religion, and energy** in Russian strategic maneuvering.

parts.title: Key Personalities and Political Dynamics

sentences: ## **Key Personalities and Political Dynamics**
**Moisés Naím** emerges as an influential figure, while different **political parties** such as the **National Bolshevik Party** and **Nashi** make their presence felt.
The intricacy of **nationalism** in both its historical and Russian contexts is apparent as it interweaves through alliances like the **National Reserve Bank** and other entities.
Organizations such as **NGOs**—focused both on **American** influence and those restricted in **Russia**—highlight ongoing tensions.
Figures like **Aleksey Navalny** and **Nursultan Nazarbayev** stand out as part of the broader **political landscape**.
